title: An HTTP Status Code for Indicating Hints
summary: This memo introduces the 103 status code, an informational HTTP status code that conveys hints to a client before the final response. The hints help the client begin preparing, for example by loading resources, while the server is still working on the full answer.

plainLanguage.summary: While the server cooks the main meal, it hands over a quick note saying, you'll want a fork and a plate, so you can set the table.

questions: how to preload resources before the final response
how does early hints differ from http2 server push
can a server send multiple 103 responses
subtitle: A provisional HTTP response that lets a server hand over hints while it is still working on the real answer.

tldr.problem: A server often cannot send the final response headers right away, for example because it is waiting on an upstream server or a database query, so the client cannot start fetching the resources it will need.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends one or more informational 103 (Early Hints) responses carrying header fields, typically Link headers with the preload relation, that are likely to appear in the final response.
tldr.outcome: Clients can speculatively start work such as fetching resources, but the hints never replace the final response's header fields. The RFC text is marked Experimental.

today: RFC 8297 has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. The RFC text itself carries the Experimental category, while the metadata lists the status as Proposed Standard.

sections.title: The Waiting Problem
sections.content:
Many HTTP responses contain links to external resources that must be fetched before use, for example when a web browser renders HTML. Having those links as early as possible helps to minimize perceived latency.

The preload link relation can carry such links in the Link header field of a response. The catch is that an origin server cannot always build the header block of the final response immediately. It might delegate the request to an upstream HTTP server at a distant location, or the status code might depend on the result of a database query. The server would like to send some header fields at once, but it cannot until the status code and the full headers of the final response are settled.
sections.plainLanguage: The server knows what the web page will need long before the page is ready. It just has no polite way to say so until the whole answer is done.

sections.title: Why Not Server Push?
sections.content:
HTTP/2 server push can also speed up delivery, but the RFC names two limits. It only works for resources the server is authoritative for, and the pushed response is sent whether or not the client already has it cached.

Delivering Link header fields early is more flexible and might consume less bandwidth, at the cost of spending one extra round trip compared to server push in the worst case. The informational response can also be used by an origin server to trigger HTTP/2 server push at a caching intermediary.
sections.plainLanguage: Pushing is like mailing someone a parcel they may already own. A hint is just a note that says what is coming, so they can say no thanks.

sections.title: The 103 Status Code
sections.content:
The 103 (Early Hints) informational status code tells the client that the server is likely to send a final response with the header fields included in the informational response. A server will typically repeat those fields in the final response, though it might not if it learns before finishing that the hints were wrong.

A client can speculatively evaluate the header fields while it waits. For example, it might see a Link value with the relation type preload and start fetching the target. The fields are only hints and do not replace the header fields on the final response.

Apart from performance optimizations, evaluating a 103 response MUST NOT affect how the final response is processed. A client MUST NOT treat its header fields as metadata about the 103 response itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is only a hint. You may start setting the table, but you must still wait for the real meal and check what actually arrives.

sections.title: Partial and Repeated Hints
sections.content:
A server MAY list only some of the header fields it expects in the final response. A client SHOULD NOT read the absence of a field from a 103 response as a sign that the field is unlikely to appear later.

A server might also send more than one 103 response before the final one. A server MAY emit several as new information becomes available while the request is processed. It does not need to repeat fields already sent, though it may. The client can consider any combination of fields from multiple 103 responses when anticipating the final one. One case the RFC gives is a caching intermediary that sends a 103 based on a stale cached response and then forwards a 103 and a final response from the origin server for a revalidation request.

In the RFC's second example, two 103 responses announce three Link header fields. The final 200 response contains two of them, and the third is replaced by a Link with a different value.
sections.plainLanguage: The waiter may come back with more notes as the cook decides things. The notes can overlap, and the final plate may differ a little from what the notes said.

sections.title: A Worked Exchange
sections.content:
In the RFC's basic example, the client sends GET / HTTP/1.1 with Host: example.com. The server first answers HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints with two Link headers asking for preloading of /style.css as a style and /script.js as a script. It then sends HTTP/1.1 200 OK with the same two Link fields, a Content-Length of 1234 and the HTML body.

The 103 response arrives first, so the client can begin fetching the two files while the server finishes producing the page.
sections.plainLanguage: The first message says, you will need these two files. The second message is the real page, and it lists the same files again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some clients may mishandle a 103 response, because informational responses are rarely used in reply to requests that do not include an Expect header field.

The serious case is an HTTP/1.1 client that treats an informational response as a final response. It is then likely to consider all responses to later requests on the same connection to be part of the final response. This might be a cross-origin information disclosure vulnerability if the client multiplexes requests to different origins onto one persistent connection. For this reason a server might refrain from sending 103 responses over HTTP/1.1 unless the client is known to handle informational responses correctly.

HTTP/2 clients are less likely to suffer from incorrect framing, since handling the response header fields does not affect how the end of the response body is determined.
sections.plainLanguage: A confused listener might think the first note was the whole answer and then mix up the next conversation. So be careful whom you send notes to.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers one entry in the HTTP Status Codes registry: code 103, description Early Hints, specification RFC 8297.
sections.plainLanguage: The number 103 was written in the official list of HTTP codes with the name Early Hints.
